title: Small Intestine Wall Anatomy: Villi, Crypts & Myenteric
description: Learn small intestine wall microanatomy across all four tunics, including absorptive villi, central lacteals, crypts of Lieberkuhn, and enteric nerve nets.
h1: Small Intestine Wall Microanatomy: Villi, Crypts and Enteric Plexuses
blurb: Four gastrointestinal wall tunics, absorptive villi with central lacteals, stem-cell crypts of Lieberkühn, and the submucosal and myenteric enteric nerve plexuses.
lead: Three nested levels of folding—circular folds, finger-like villi, and microscopic brush-border microvilli—turn the inner lining of the small intestine into a vast absorptive surface. In this illustrated guide to small intestine wall microanatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including villus, crypt of lieberkühn, enterocyte, brush border—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Three nested levels of folding—circular folds, finger-like villi, and microscopic brush-border microvilli—turn the inner lining of the small intestine into a vast absorptive surface. The small-intestinal wall has mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis externa (inner circular and outer longitudinal layers) and serosa/adventitia depending on site. Villi expand surface area and crypts house renewing stem cells, antimicrobial Paneth cells and secretory lineages. Enterocytes absorb nutrients; goblet cells secrete mucus; enteroendocrine cells release signals. The submucosal plexus regulates local secretion/flow, while the myenteric plexus between muscle layers coordinates motility. These locations are different from the intestinal lumen. Within the human body, the small intestine · wall & enteric plexuses (Tunicae intestini tenuis · plexus enterici) is situated in small bowel from luminal epithelium through mucosa, submucosa, muscularis and serosa, receives arterial perfusion via mesenteric arterial branches → villus capillaries; lacteals carry dietary lipids, and is innervated by myenteric and submucosal enteric plexuses modulated by vagal/sympathetic input.

Structurally, the villus (Villus intestinalis) comprises fingerlike projection of small-intestinal mucosa with epithelial cover and lamina propria core. Physiologically, the villus expands absorptive surface. Structurally, the crypt of Lieberkühn (Glandula intestinalis) comprises epithelial invagination between villus bases toward muscularis mucosae. Physiologically, the crypt of Lieberkühn houses stem and secretory cell niches. Structurally, the enterocyte (Enterocytus) comprises absorptive columnar epithelial cell with apical microvilli. Physiologically, the enterocyte governs takes up digested nutrients. The brush border (Limbus striatus) is dense apical microvilli on enterocytes, not the large villi themselves. Physiologically, the brush border governs increases membrane area and supports digestive enzymes. Structurally, the goblet cell (Cellula caliciformis) comprises mucin-producing epithelial cell scattered among enterocytes. Physiologically, the goblet cell lubricates and helps protect mucosal surface. Structurally, the paneth cell (Cellula Paneth) comprises granule-rich cell near base of small-intestinal crypt. Physiologically, the paneth cell produces antimicrobial molecules supporting stem-cell niche.

Clinically, regarding the villus, typical colon lacks villi. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the crypt of Lieberkühn, crypt loss can impair epithelial renewal. In clinical pathology involving the enterocyte, loss of brush-border surface impairs absorption. Medical evaluation of the brush border also notes that villus and microvillus are different scales.

questions.question: What are the layers of the small intestinal wall?
questions.answer: From lumen outward they include mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa and serosa or adventitia depending on the segment. Structurally, the villus (Villus intestinalis) comprises fingerlike projection of small-intestinal mucosa with epithelial cover and lamina propria core. Physiologically, the villus expands absorptive surface.

questions.question: What do intestinal villi and crypts do?
questions.answer: Villi expand the absorptive surface. Crypts contain renewing epithelial cells and other specialized cells that help maintain the mucosa. Structurally, the crypt stem cells (Cellulae stipitales cryptarum) comprises progenitor population near crypt base continuously renewing epithelium. Physiologically, the crypt stem cells governs replaces short-lived epithelial lineages.

questions.question: What is the villus?
questions.answer: Fingerlike projection of small-intestinal mucosa with epithelial cover and lamina propria core. Functionally, it expands absorptive surface. Structurally, the enterocyte (Enterocytus) comprises absorptive columnar epithelial cell with apical microvilli. Physiologically, the enterocyte governs takes up digested nutrients.

questions.question: Where is the enterocyte located?
questions.answer: Absorptive columnar epithelial cell with apical microvilli. Functionally, it governs takes up digested nutrients. Structurally, the enteroendocrine cell (Cellula enteroendocrina) comprises scattered hormone-secreting epithelial cells. Physiologically, the enteroendocrine cell governs sense nutrients and release regulatory peptides.

questions.question: What is the function of the goblet cell?
questions.answer: Functionally, it lubricates and helps protect mucosal surface. Mucin-producing epithelial cell scattered among enterocytes. Clinically, regarding the goblet cell, cell proportions vary along intestine.
